title: The Letters to the Kings
year: late 6 AH to 7 AH — 628 CE, the months after al-Hudaybiyah
teaser: From an oasis with a mud-brick mosque, eight men rode out carrying the same short letter to eight thrones.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: A silver seal and no army coming
layers.content:
The truce had done what no battle managed. Quraysh, the bitterest enemy the call had, withdrew from the arena of war and put their name to a document. One leg of the alliance against Madinah — Quraysh, Ghatafan, and the Jews — was broken, and because Quraysh had carried the banner of paganism in Arabia, the aggressive feeling of the other pagan tribes noticeably cooled. Ghatafan alone were no great threat; their provocations had mostly been instigated from elsewhere. The Jewish leadership expelled from Madinah had gone north to Khaybar and was working there.

Al-Mubarakpuri divides what followed the treaty into two streams: continuous peaceful effort in propagating the call, and military activity. The Muslims gave the first a clear preference over the second.

Late in the sixth year of the Hijra, returning from al-Hudaybiyah, the Prophet ﷺ decided to write to the kings beyond Arabia. To authenticate the credentials of the men who would carry the letters, a silver seal was made, engraved in three lines with three words: Muhammad, Messenger, Allah. Sahih al-Bukhari records it. Envoys were chosen on the basis of their experience and their knowledge, and sent out in Muharram of the seventh year — a few days before the army marched on Khaybar.

Consider who was being written to. Persia and Byzantium had spent the preceding decades tearing each other apart across Syria and Iraq, and between them they governed the settled world from the Nile to Khorasan. Egypt was Byzantine and Coptic. Abyssinia was a Christian kingdom across the water. Bahrain, Yamamah, Damascus, and Oman answered to one empire or the other.

Madinah was a date-palm oasis with a mosque of stone and adobe brick and a roof of palm leaves. The letters went out anyway.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — the Prophet's silver seal
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: Eight Roads Out of Arabia
layers.subtitle: Almost the same letter, eight times over
layers.content:
The Sealed Nectar names the bearer and the throne for each. 'Amr bin Umayyah ad-Damri to the Negus of Abyssinia. Hatib bin Abi Balta'ah to al-Muqawqis at Alexandria. Abdullah bin Hudhafah as-Sahmi to Chosroes of Persia. Dihyah bin Khalifah al-Kalbi to Heraclius, handed first to the governor of Busra to pass on. Al-'Ala' bin al-Hadrami to al-Mundhir bin Sawa in Bahrain. Sulait bin 'Amr al-'Amiri to Haudhah bin 'Ali in Yamamah. Shuja' bin Wahb to al-Harith bin Abi Shimr al-Ghassani in Damascus. 'Amr bin al-'As to Jaifer and 'Abd, the sons of al-Julandai, in Oman.

The letters are short, and they are nearly the same letter. Each opens: peace be upon him who follows true guidance. Then the invitation — accept Islam and you will be secure; accept it and Allah will reward you twice over; refuse it, and the burden of your whole people's rejection falls on your shoulders. To several of them the verse was added: «قُلْ يَا أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ تَعَالَوْا إِلَى كَلِمَةٍ سَوَاءٍ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَكُمْ أَلَّا نَعْبُدَ إِلَّا اللَّهَ» — 'Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is just between us and you, that we worship none but Allah.' (3:64)

Notice what is not in them. No tribute. No territory. No demand that a throne be vacated. To Mundhir of Bahrain, to Haudhah of Yamamah, to al-Harith of Damascus, and to the brothers in Oman he wrote in one form or another that their command would remain theirs.

The dating is not clean, and the sources say so. At-Tabari places the letter to the Negus late in the sixth or early in the seventh year, while al-Mubarakpuri reads the surviving text as one written years earlier, during the emigration to Abyssinia, because it commends Ja'far and his companions to the king's care. The letter to Oman he judges to have gone out much later, most likely after Makkah was opened. What the sources agree on is the campaign, not the calendar.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Parchment and the Pieces
layers.subtitle: One king raised it to his eye, one tore it up
layers.content:
Two men received the same kind of letter, and the distance between what they did with it is the whole chapter.

'Amr bin Umayyah reached the court of Abyssinia. The Negus — Ashamah bin al-Abjar — took the parchment, placed it against his eye, came down from his seat to the floor, and declared his faith. His written reply is preserved: I have received your letter in which you have mentioned Jesus, and by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, Jesus is no more than what you say. We fully acknowledge that with which you have been sent to us, and we have entertained your cousin and his companions. He closed by surrendering himself, through Ja'far, to the Lord of the worlds. He was asked to send the emigrants home, and they came back to find the Prophet ﷺ at Khaybar.

Abdullah bin Hudhafah's letter travelled the other way. Chosroes was filled with anger at its style, because the Prophet's name had been placed above his own. He tore it to pieces. Then he wrote to Badhan, his governor in Yemen, ordering him to send two men to arrest this Arab and bring him to Persia.

The two men reached Madinah. Before they could act, the Prophet ﷺ told them what he had been given to know: that Pervez, emperor of Persia, had been murdered by his own son. They were stunned. He told them to carry a message to their new king — that Islam would prevail everywhere and would exceed the kingdom of Chosroes himself.

They hurried back to Badhan. A letter from Sherweh, the new king, arrived confirming the death and ordering Badhan to suspend all proceedings against the Prophet ﷺ until further notice. Badhan, and the Persians in Yemen with him, entered Islam.

One man kissed a letter. One tore it, and his empire's southern province changed religion before his successor could write again.
layers.hadith_ref: Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari — the letter to Chosroes and the news of Pervez's death, cited in The Sealed Nectar
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Word That Was Just Between Them
layers.subtitle: The verse the letters carried, and two given in reply
layers.content:
No revelation is recorded as having been sent down about the letters themselves. The decision to write was the Prophet's own governance. But the verse the letters carried was chosen, and it repays reading twice.

«قُلْ يَا أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ تَعَالَوْا إِلَى كَلِمَةٍ سَوَاءٍ بَيْنَنَا وَبَيْنَكُمْ أَلَّا نَعْبُدَ إِلَّا اللَّهَ» — 'Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is just between us and you, that we worship none but Allah, and that we associate no partners with Him, and that none of us shall take others as lords besides Allah.' Then the clause that ends the argument when it is refused: 'Then, if they turn away, say: Bear witness that we are Muslims.' (3:64)

It does not open with the differences. It opens with the ground already held in common, states it as a word that is just — equal — between the two sides, and adds a third clause aimed at every court it was read in: that no man shall take another man as a lord. Then it stops. There is no threat and no bargaining after it. The invitation states its terms and rests.

Behind the whole campaign stands the verse that made it necessary: «قُلْ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إِنِّي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ إِلَيْكُمْ جَمِيعًا» — 'Say: O mankind, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all.' (7:158) He wrote to Chosroes in exactly those terms: I am the Messenger of Allah sent to all people.

Two pieces of revelation are recorded during the episode, and both concerned the recipients rather than the letters. The first was the death of Pervez, known in Madinah before any rider could carry it. The second came about Haudhah bin 'Ali of Yamamah, who had replied that he was a famous orator and poet whom the Arabs respected, and would follow if he were given a place in the government. Jibreel brought word that Haudhah had died. On that news the Prophet ﷺ said that from Yamamah would come a liar claiming prophethood after him, and that he would be killed. Asked who would kill him, he answered: you and your companions.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: What arrived, what was refused, what came true
layers.content:
Al-Muqawqis of Egypt read the letter and said this Prophet proposed nothing repulsive — neither a straying magician nor a lying soothsayer, but a man bearing the true manifest seeds of prophethood. He placed the parchment in an ivory casket, wrote back that he had expected the awaited Prophet in Syria, and sent presents instead of an answer: two maids of noble Coptic families, clothing, and a mount. Mariyah bore the Prophet's son Ibrahim. Sirin was given to the poet Hassan bin Thabit. The mount was Duldul, which lived into Mu'awiyah's time. He never accepted Islam.

Heraclius went further and stopped in the same place. He summoned Abu Sufyan, trading in Sham under the truce, and cross-examined him about his kinsman; al-Bukhari preserves it on the authority of Ibn Abbas. Abu Sufyan — still an enemy — said the man came of a noble family in which no king had risen, that his followers were the weak and kept increasing, that none of them left him, that he neither lied nor betrayed, and that he ordered prayer, honesty, abstinence, and the keeping of family ties. Heraclius took the answers apart before his court and concluded: if this is true, he will soon rule the place beneath my feet; if I were with him, I would wash his feet. Then the letter was read aloud, the room turned tense, and the clergy were ordered out. He never became a Muslim.

The other replies ran the full range. Mundhir kept Bahrain and asked what to do with the Magians and Jews among his people. Al-Harith of Damascus demanded to know who dared depose him. Jaifer of Oman kept 'Amr bin al-'As waiting at his door and threatened him, then spoke with his brother, and both accepted.

Carry this. Haudhah named his price and was refused, though a governor's conversion was worth having. The land, the Prophet ﷺ answered, is in the Hand of Allah, Who gives it to whom He wills. Years later 'Adi bin Hatim, who had heard him promise that men would open the treasures of Kisra, said: I was one of those who opened them.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn Abbas — Heraclius and Abu Sufyan; Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by 'Adi bin Hatim — the treasures of Kisra
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: A silver seal was made so the envoys could authenticate the letters they carried. What was engraved on it?

options.text: The words 'Muhammad the Messenger of Allah', in three lines
The first verse of Surah al-Fatihah
The name of the city of Madinah
Nothing — the letters were sealed with wax only

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Prophet's Plans to Spread the Message of Islam Beyond Arabia
quiz.scholar_reflection: Three words on a ring. The letters were going to men who ruled from the Nile to Khorasan, and this was the entire apparatus of state behind them.

quiz.prompt: Which ruler took the letter, placed it against his eye, came down from his seat to the floor, and declared his faith?

options.text: Al-Muqawqis, the ruler of Egypt
Heraclius, emperor of the Byzantines
The Negus of Abyssinia, Ashamah bin al-Abjar
Al-Harith bin Abi Shimr al-Ghassani of Damascus

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Letter to Abyssinia, with the Negus's written reply
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had already sheltered the emigrants years earlier without accepting their faith. The reply he wrote settles it: I bear witness that you are the Messenger of Allah, true and confirming those who have gone before you.

quiz.prompt: Chosroes tore up the letter and ordered his governor in Yemen to have the Prophet ﷺ arrested. What happened when the two arresting men reached Madinah?

options.text: They were imprisoned until Persia sent a ransom
The Prophet ﷺ told them Pervez had been murdered by his own son, which a letter from Persia soon confirmed
They were sent back with a second letter to Chosroes
They found the city empty, as the army had gone to Khaybar

quiz.citation: Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Letter to Chosroes, Emperor of Persia
quiz.scholar_reflection: Badhan, the governor who had sent them, entered Islam along with the Persians in Yemen. The order to arrest one man ended by removing a province from the empire that gave it.

quiz.prompt: Haudhah bin 'Ali of Yamamah wrote back that the faith he was invited to was very good. What condition did he attach to following it?

options.text: That the Muslims stop trading through his territory
That he be included in the government
That the Prophet ﷺ come to Yamamah in person
That his poetry be recited in the mosque at Madinah

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Letter to Haudhah bin 'Ali, the Governor of Yamamah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He described himself as a famous orator and poet whom the Arabs respected. The demand was refused: the Prophet ﷺ answered that the whole matter was in the Hand of Allah, Who gives His land to whom He wills.

quiz.prompt: Al-Muqawqis of Egypt judged the letter sincere, kept it in an ivory casket, and sent presents in return. What did he do about the invitation itself?

options.text: He accepted Islam and had the letter read publicly in Alexandria
He rejected it outright and expelled the envoy
He said he would consider the matter deeply, and did not accept it
He forwarded it to Heraclius and let him decide

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Letter to the King of Egypt, Muqawqis
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar puts it bluntly: he did not avail himself of this priceless opportunity. He said the coming of a Prophet was still due but that he had expected him in Syria, and sent gifts instead of an answer.

quiz.prompt: Heraclius dismantled every objection in front of his own court, said that if this were true the man would soon rule the ground beneath his feet, and did not follow him. What do you think held him?

options.text: The throne — he could see the cost of belief priced in his own crown
The room he was standing in; his clergy would not have survived it
He was impressed but never actually convinced, and impressed is cheap
Knowing a thing and acting on it are separate faculties in a person

quiz.slider_label: He never really believed — He believed and refused
quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by Ibn Abbas — Heraclius's questioning of Abu Sufyan, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: By his own account he had already known a Prophet would arise. What he said he had not expected was that he would be an Arab. He added: if I were sure, I would be faithful to him.

quiz.prompt: The same short letter, with the same terms, went to a king who raised it to his eye and to a king who tore it to pieces. What does refusing to tailor the message tell you?

options.text: A message that is adjusted for each listener is no longer one message
It treats an emperor and a small governor as the same size of person
It was a missed chance — Chosroes might have read a gentler letter
The point was to leave every one of them without an excuse

quiz.slider_label: Speak to each in his own language — Say the same thing to all
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the texts of the eight letters
quiz.scholar_reflection: The one adjustment that does appear is the closing warning, shaped to each man's responsibility: the sins of the Copts, of the Magians, of your own people. The invitation itself never moved.

quiz.prompt: Haudhah's conversion would have brought a whole region in, and his price was only a share in government. It was refused. Where do you sit on paying that kind of price?

options.text: Refuse it — a man bought with office will need buying again
Pay it — the region matters more than the principle
The refusal was about who grants authority, not about strategy at all
I would have negotiated it down rather than refused outright

quiz.slider_label: Take the region — Keep the terms
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Prophet's reply to Haudhah bin 'Ali
quiz.scholar_reflection: Note what he did offer freely, unasked: Mundhir kept Bahrain, the brothers kept Oman, al-Harith was told his kingdom would remain his. Office was not the thing being withheld. Being owed it was.

quiz.prompt: The letters demanded no tribute, no land, and no throne — several explicitly left the ruler in command of his own country. How do you read that?

options.text: It proves the aim was the faith and not the territory
It was realistic — Madinah could not have taken any of these countries
Leaving a hostile ruler in place stores up the next war
Removing the political cost is how you make a real choice possible

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the letters to Mundhir bin Sawa, Haudhah bin 'Ali, al-Harith al-Ghassani, and the sons of al-Julandai
quiz.scholar_reflection: The one line that reads like pressure is in the letter to Oman, and even there it is conditional on refusal. Every letter offers safety first, in the same words: accept Islam and you will be secure.

quiz.prompt: A year earlier he had been turned back from his own birthplace and had signed a treaty his companions found bitter. Now he wrote to two empires. What does that ordering say about how he read his own position?

options.text: He measured himself by what he had been sent with, not by what he held
The treaty was the opening — peace with Quraysh freed him to look outward
It looks like overreach, and it happened to succeed
Waiting until the position looked adequate would have meant waiting forever

quiz.slider_label: Build the strength first — Send the letters now
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — A New Phase of Islamic Action
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar dates the decision to the return journey from al-Hudaybiyah itself. He did not wait for the ink of the treaty to dry before deciding that Arabia was too small a field.
